The outcome

Wool on the mould cells

C12 + C13 · v7

The slime mould’s cells, taken step by step to a road network: the cells on the vein centrelines, the existing roads and towns that cut them, the soil that splits them again, the anchors, the net, the wool relaxing live, and the road hierarchy and parcels it gives. This side changes the outcome; the right side changes only how it looks.

How the roads are read

Anchors

Click a primary cell’s edge to add an anchor. Drag one to move it along the edge. Right-click one to delete it.
Anchor spacing
The anchors between the road anchors, along each primary cell’s edge.
Near the station, spacing
Finer near the station, back to the full spacing 3 km out.
On good soil, spacing
Grade 1 and 2 are kept for farming, so the net is looser there.

The wool

Magnet
How strongly nearby threads pull together into bundles.
Angle
How much each thread resists bending.
Relaxation steps

The road hierarchy

Continuity angle
At a junction, two streets are one road if one carries on within this angle of straight. Lower: straighter, shorter roads.
Existing road corridor
No new road runs along an existing one inside this width: the threads there merge into the existing road. B roads use 60% of it.
A road reach
Every place should be within this of an A road or the cell edge: a third more on Grade 1–2 farmland, a fifth less within 3 km of the station. A roads are added, one at a time, where most land is out of reach.
A roads apart
No A road runs alongside another M or A road closer than this; crossing is allowed. An A road is at least 2.5 km long.
B: share of the roads left
Whole roads, busiest and longest first, never alongside an A or M; the rest are C.
Fillet at junctions
The inside corner where two roads meet, rounded to this radius (step 12); the parcels keep the same corners (step 13).
